pl-l2d38c3-d1e108.summary: Asks whether all good wills have one end only.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e111.summary: Cites De Trinitate XI: different wills have their own ends, referred to the end of the will to live blessedly, which suffices by itself; the will to see has vision as end, the will to see a window has seeing the window, and the will to see passersby through it has seeing them; these are referred to that end.
claims: Wills have proper ends referred to beatitude.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e116.summary: Continues: wills are right and linked if the one to which all are referred is good; if it is wrong, all are wrong; the connection of right wills is a path of ascent to beatitude by sure steps; the entanglement of wrong wills is a chain binding one to be cast into outer darkness.
claims: The final will determines the rightness of all.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e120.summary: Concludes that the faithful have many right wills with proper and diverse ends, yet one end, since all refer to the end of ends; perhaps likewise conversely in the wicked.
claims: Many ends are referred to one end.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e123.summary: Notes the apparent conflict with De sermone Domini: we should not preach to eat but eat to preach; 'seek first the kingdom of God, and all these will be added' means not seeking these too, lest we set two ends, the kingdom for itself and necessities for it; so all should be done for the kingdom only, not with temporal reward in view.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e128.summary: States the tension: here Augustine says not to set two ends but one, the kingdom of God, while above he said different good wills have their own ends.

pl-l2d38c3-d1e131.summary: Resolves it: the same Augustine said we eat to preach, making the Gospel the end of eating and referring it to the kingdom; so two ends, and no sin. He forbids ends tending in different directions, not referred to one another; and temporal reward is not to be sought for itself with the kingdom, but for the kingdom. Asking temporal things for eternal life does not offend, the left hand under the head and the right embracing; seeking them for themselves mixes left with right. So 'do not do your justice before men' and 'let your light shine before men' agree; all is to be done for God, referring all ends to him.
claims: Temporal goods are sought rightly for eternal life.

pl-l2d38c3.summary: Asks whether all good wills have one end. Augustine: different wills have their own ends, referred to the end of the will to live blessedly, as the will to see a window has its end, and the will to see passersby through it another; right wills linked to a good final will form a path of ascent to beatitude, wrong wills a chain binding to outer darkness. So good wills have proper and diverse ends yet one end of ends. This seems to conflict with Augustine's warning not to set two ends ('we should eat to preach, not preach to eat'; 'seek first the kingdom'), but Lombard resolves it: he forbids ends not referred to one another, not subordinate ends; asking temporal things for the sake of eternal life is no offense, but seeking them for themselves mixes the left hand with the right.
claims: Different good wills have their own ends.
All good wills are referred to the one end, beatitude.
Right wills form a path to beatitude; wrong wills a chain to darkness.
Augustine forbids two unrelated ends, not subordinate ends.
Temporal goods may be sought for the sake of eternal life, not for themselves.
